COMMERCIAL LEASE ASSIGNMENT AND SUBLETTING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Lee Consulting, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California statutory law and case law on a tenant's ability to assign or sublease its interest in a commercial lease of the property at 500 Commerce Way, Suite 200, Springfield, CA between Acme Properties, LLC, as landlord, and Jordan Lee Consulting, Inc., as tenant, and on the standards that govern a landlord's consent when the lease requires it. The statutory chapter this information sheet describes, by its own terms, applies only to a lease of real property for other than residential purposes. This information sheet states what California law provides on this subject. It does not authorize, direct, or prohibit any particular assignment, sublease, or withholding of consent, and it does not tell either Acme Properties, LLC or Jordan Lee Consulting, Inc. what to do about any specific proposed transfer.

THREE KINDS OF TRANSFER RESTRICTION A COMMERCIAL LEASE MAY CONTAIN
California's Civil Code defines a "restriction on transfer" as a lease provision that restricts a commercial tenant's right to transfer its interest in the lease, and separately defines "transfer" to include an assignment, a sublease, or another voluntary or involuntary transfer or encumbrance of all or part of that interest. Within that framework, California law recognizes three distinct kinds of restriction a commercial lease may impose. First, a restriction may absolutely prohibit transfer outright. Second, a restriction may allow transfer but make it subject to an express standard or condition set out in the lease, which can include a provision entitling the landlord to some or all of any consideration the tenant receives from a transferee above the rent under the lease. Third, a restriction may require the landlord's consent for transfer, subject to an express standard or condition for giving or withholding that consent — including, without limitation, a standard that consent may not be unreasonably withheld, or a standard that consent may be withheld subject to express conditions the lease itself sets out.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "“Restriction on transfer” means a provision in a lease that restricts the right of transfer of the tenant’s interest in the lease."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, defining "restriction on transfer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.020.)
  "A restriction on transfer of a tenant’s interest in a lease may absolutely prohibit transfer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.230 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, a restriction may absolutely prohibit transfer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.230.)
  "A restriction on transfer of a tenant’s interest in a lease may provide that the transfer is subject to any express standard or condition, including, but not limited to, a provision that the landlord is entitled to some or all of any consideration the tenant receives from a transferee in excess of the rent under the lease."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.240 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, a restriction may impose an express standard or condition, including a landlord profit-sharing provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.240.)
  "A restriction on transfer of a tenant’s interest in a lease may require the landlord’s consent for transfer subject to any express standard or condition for giving or withholding consent, including, but not limited to, either of the following: (a) The landlord’s consent may not be unreasonably withheld. (b) The landlord’s consent may be withheld subject to express standards or conditions."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.250 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, a restriction may require consent subject to an express standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.250.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of the range of transfer restrictions California law permits in a commercial lease — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's lease; whether a jurisdiction permits an absolute prohibition on transfer, and what forms of consent standard it allows a lease to specify, vary by state. The four citations below are drawn from the same statutory chapter (Civil Code §§ 1995.020(c), 1995.230, 1995.240, 1995.250) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for the three-category structure itself. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific transfer restriction, and it does not determine whether any particular lease provision falls into one of these categories or is enforceable as written.

THE IMPLIED REASONABLENESS STANDARD WHEN A LEASE REQUIRES CONSENT BUT STATES NO STANDARD
If a commercial lease's restriction on transfer requires the landlord's consent but states no standard at all for giving or withholding that consent, California law construes the restriction to include an implied standard that the landlord's consent may not be unreasonably withheld. Whether consent was unreasonably withheld in a particular case is a question of fact, and California law places the burden of proof on that question on the tenant. California law also identifies one specific way a tenant can satisfy that burden: by showing that, in response to the tenant's written request for a statement of reasons for withholding consent, the landlord failed, within a reasonable time, to state a reasonable objection to the transfer in writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "If a restriction on transfer of the tenant’s interest in a lease requires the landlord’s consent for transfer but provides no standard for giving or withholding consent, the restriction on transfer shall be construed to include an implied standard that the landlord’s consent may not be unreasonably withheld."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.260 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the implied not-unreasonably-withheld standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.260.)
  "Whether the landlord’s consent has been unreasonably withheld in a particular case is a question of fact on which the tenant has the burden of proof. The tenant may satisfy the burden of proof by showing that, in response to the tenant’s written request for a statement of reasons for withholding consent, the landlord has failed, within a reasonable time, to state in writing a reasonable objection to the transfer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.260 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the tenant's burden of proof and one way to satisfy it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.260.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's default consent standard and burden of proof — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's lease; whether a jurisdiction implies a reasonableness standard into a silent consent clause, and who bears the burden of proving unreasonableness, vary by state. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory subsection (§ 1995.260) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This standard's applicability to a specific lease can also be affected by the statute's own retroactivity limit, addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine whether any specific landlord's consent was or would be unreasonably withheld, or whether any specific tenant has met its burden of proof.

KENDALL V. ERNEST PESTANA: THE "COMMERCIALLY REASONABLE OBJECTION" STANDARD
Before this statutory scheme was enacted, the California Supreme Court decided Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., addressing whether a commercial landlord could arbitrarily withhold consent to an assignment where the lease required consent but stated no standard for it. Rejecting the older "majority rule" that had allowed arbitrary withholding, the court adopted what it called the minority rule. The court held that where a commercial lease provides for assignment only with the landlord's prior consent, and states no standard for that consent, the landlord's consent may be withheld only where the landlord has a commercially reasonable objection to the assignee or the proposed use.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "For the reasons discussed below, we conclude that the minority rule is the preferable position."
  — Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 496-497 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, adopting the minority rule against arbitrary withholding of consent (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1282333/kendall-v-ernest-pestana-inc/)
  "In conclusion, both the policy against restraints on alienation and the implied contractual duty of good faith and fair dealing militate in favor of adoption of the rule that where a commercial lease provides for assignment only with the prior consent of the lessor, such consent may be withheld only where the lessor has a commercially reasonable objection to the assignee or the proposed use."
  — Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 506-507 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, the commercially-reasonable-objection holding (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1282333/kendall-v-ernest-pestana-inc/)
  Known gap: This is one state's case law, used as evidence of the judicial rule that preceded, and that the Legislature has since largely codified through Civil Code § 1995.260, addressed in a separate clause of this document — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's lease. Both citations below are drawn from the same opinion (Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc. (1985) 40 Cal.3d 488) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for the court's own holding. A genuine, correctable source-formatting artifact was found and fixed: the html_with_citations text CourtListener returns for this opinion embeds a mid-word pagination marker (a `<page-number>` tag reading "*507") splitting the word "assignee" as "as"+"signee" at the page 506-507 break; this quote removes that embedded pagination marker (verified as a formatting artifact, not missing or altered substantive text, against two independent fetches of the opinion) rather than reproducing the split word. Separately, the court's opinion by its own terms addressed only a commercial lease and expressly declined to decide whether its holding extends to a residential lease. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine whether any specific landlord's objection to a specific assignee or proposed use was or would be commercially reasonable.

WHICH LEASES THE IMPLIED STANDARD APPLIES TO
California's implied not-unreasonably-withheld standard, described elsewhere in this document, does not apply to every silent consent-to-transfer clause regardless of when it was written. By its own terms, that implied standard applies to a restriction on transfer executed on or after September 23, 1983. For a restriction on transfer executed before that date that requires the landlord's consent but states no standard, California law instead provides that the landlord's consent may be unreasonably withheld. For this purpose, if the terms of a restriction on transfer are fixed by an option or other agreement, California law deems the restriction executed on the date that option or other agreement was executed, not the date the lease itself was later signed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Section 1995.260 applies to a restriction on transfer executed on or after September 23, 1983. If a restriction on transfer executed before September 23, 1983, requires the landlord’s consent for the tenant’s transfer but provides no standard for giving or withholding consent, the landlord’s consent may be unreasonably withheld. For purposes of this subdivision, if the terms of a restriction on transfer are fixed by an option or other agreement, the restriction on transfer is deemed to be executed on the date of execution of the option or other agreement."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.270(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the September 23, 1983 retroactivity boundary for the implied standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1995.270.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of the specific date boundary California law sets for its implied consent standard — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's lease, and not a claim that every state's version of this doctrine (to the extent one exists) carries the same or any retroactivity limit. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1995.270(b)); no additional independent source was found for this specific date threshold, though the date itself (September 23, 1983) corresponds to the date of the Court of Appeal's decision in Cohen v. Ratinoff (1983) 147 Cal.App.3d 321, a case referenced in the Legislature's own findings elsewhere in this same statutory section. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine when any specific lease's restriction on transfer was executed for purposes of this date boundary.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding assignment and subletting of the leased premises at 500 Commerce Way, Suite 200, Springfield, CA, leased by Acme Properties, LLC to Jordan Lee Consulting, Inc., states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any particular proposed transfer.
